Classical commentators note the shift from answering the accusation to diagnosing it. What is offered as the real reason is not confusion about the messenger's sanity but a settled dislike of what he was saying.

keyTerms.note: A word for finding something repugnant rather than for judging it false. Naming aversion instead of doubt relocates the whole dispute from the mind to the disposition.
From a root meaning to fall or to drop. What the word names is not appetite but the pull of a preference, and its image is of something descending rather than being chosen.
The verb for something wholesome turning corrupt, used of food, of water and of social order alike. The claim is of decay rather than of collapse, a system spoiling from within.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meccan society ran on consensus reached in council, where the strongest interests generally prevailed and the outcome was then treated as the right answer. That was how the sanctuary was managed, how disputes were settled, and how the calendar was adjusted when it suited the trade. A claim that truth does not bend to what people want was aimed directly at the mechanism by which the city decided things.
studies.didYouKnow: The same word for madness is used against this messenger and against Noah earlier in this surah, so the chapter's first accusation and its last are identical. The reply here does not defend his sanity at all. It moves straight past the charge to say that most of them dislike the truth, which the classical commentators read as answering the motive rather than the words.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Truth is described as having a structure that the world depends on, so bending it is not a local adjustment but a general corruption. That is a strong claim and the passage makes it in one clause. It also drops the last word of the exchange back on the accusers, who are said to have been given their own reminder and to be turning away from it, which makes the refusal self-inflicted rather than imposed.

crossReferences.why: Describes someone who has taken his own desire as his god, the arrangement this ayah rules out.
Warns against following inclinations after knowledge has come, in the same vocabulary of desire.
Puts the identical charge of madness in the mouth of Noah's people, earlier in this surah.

studies.applyIt: Notice one belief you hold that costs you nothing and flatters you slightly. Everyone has several. You do not need to abandon it today. Just ask honestly whether you would still hold it if it were inconvenient, and let the answer sit. That question is the whole of what this ayah is doing.

studies.title: Are You Asking Them For Payment
studies.meaning: One possible motive remains and the passage closes it. Or are you asking them for a payment, when your Lord's return is better, and He is the best of providers. The commentators note that the question is put to the messenger rather than about him, so the answer is left to the audience who already knew he charged nothing. Then two flat statements. You are calling them to a straight path, and those who do not believe in the hereafter are veering off it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a city where every claim was assessed for the advantage behind it. Classical commentators observe that the Quran repeatedly has messengers state that they seek no wage, and that here the point is made as a question the listeners could answer from their own observation of a man they had known for forty years before he said anything.

keyTerms.note: Something paid out of what one has. The word occurs twice in the Quran, and in the other place a frightened people offer it to a passing ruler for a wall, and he declines to take it.
From the same root as the payment being refused, but naming what comes in rather than what goes out. The ayah sets the two words side by side and prefers the one that comes from God.
From a verb for turning off a course, used of a camel that drifts from the track. The word occurs once in the Quran, and it describes deviation rather than a decision to go elsewhere.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Poets took money. So did soothsayers, orators who spoke for a clan, and men who arranged a marriage or a settlement. Payment for words was normal and expected, which made it the first question anyone would ask about a new speaker. A man who kept saying difficult things for years while collecting nothing was an anomaly the city could see for itself, and the ayah simply points at it.
studies.didYouKnow: The two words for payment in this ayah come from one root, and the second is not the more usual word for a reward. What is set against the payment he is not asking for is a return of the same kind, from a different source. The word he is not asking for occurs only twice in the Quran, and the other place has a ruler refusing exactly the same offer.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Sincerity is tested here by an absence rather than by a declaration. Nobody is asked to inspect the messenger's heart; they are asked what he has taken, which is a public fact. The passage then names the consequence of ignoring that evidence, and the word chosen is one for drifting off a track rather than for choosing another road, which locates the failure in inattention rather than in defiance.

crossReferences.why: A ruler is offered payment for building a barrier and refuses it, using the same word for the payment.
Noah states that he asks no wage for the message, and that his reward is with the Lord of the worlds.
A man urges his town to follow messengers who ask them for no payment at all.

studies.applyIt: Look at one thing you do for others and ask what you take for it. Not money necessarily: credit, gratitude, the story you get to tell about yourself. Then try doing it once this week with the payment removed. Whatever discomfort shows up is a fairly reliable measure of what you were collecting.

studies.title: They Did Not Yield
studies.meaning: A hypothetical is put and answered: even if We had mercy on them and lifted the harm they were in, they would keep on wandering in their overreach. Then the fact, which is harder. We already seized them with suffering, and they neither yielded to their Lord nor pleaded with Him. The commentators note the two verbs. Yielding and pleading are the ordinary human responses to trouble, and the passage records their absence rather than any act of defiance.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the classical commentators connect the suffering mentioned here to a hard period of drought and shortage that the city endured while the message was being rejected. Reports about its length and severity vary and the sources record the variation. What the ayat establish is the response rather than the event: hardship arrived, and the expected turning did not follow it.

keyTerms.note: To keep pushing on in something, from a root also used of a deep sea. The verb appears once in the Quran, and it describes continuing rather than beginning, so relief would only extend what was already running.
To become still and lowly before someone. The word carries a physical image of a body going quiet, and its absence here is described as a failure of posture rather than of belief.
A state of falling mute because there is nothing left to say. The word names the exhaustion of hope rather than grief, and it arrives only when the gate of severe punishment opens.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Drought was how that world learned to pray. When wells sank and pasture failed, whole communities went out to the open ground to ask for rain, and the practice long predated the message. Everyone understood suffering as the moment you humbled yourself, because there was nothing else to do. A city that went through shortage without that turning would have been noticed by its own people.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for persisting in defiance occurs only here in the Quran. The verb for pleading occurs twice, and its other appearance says that God seized earlier peoples with hardship so that they might plead. That ayah gives the purpose of affliction, and this one records a case where the purpose was not achieved.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Hardship is described as an invitation rather than as a verdict, and its failure is stated without any suggestion that it should have worked automatically. That is an honest position. It also removes a comfortable assumption on the other side: suffering does not by itself produce humility, and neither does relief produce gratitude, since the passage has just said that lifting the harm would change nothing at all.

crossReferences.why: States that earlier peoples were seized with hardship so that they might plead, the purpose named here.
Describes the same sequence, hardship then ease, and the forgetting that follows the relief.
Uses the same rare word for those struck silent, in a scene where an appeal is finally made.

studies.applyIt: Think back to the last genuinely hard stretch you had, and ask what it changed. Not what you learned in hindsight, what actually changed in how you live. If the honest answer is very little, that is worth knowing now rather than after the next one. Difficulty only teaches people who let it.

studies.title: Hearing, Sight And Hearts
studies.meaning: The argument turns from history to the reader's own equipment. He is the one who produced for you hearing, sight and hearts, and then a short clause with no softening: little is the thanks you give. Then a second sentence in the same shape. He is the one who scattered you across the earth, and to Him you will be gathered. The commentators note the pairing of scattering and gathering, which uses one image for both ends of a life.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has spent its length on peoples who would not listen, and this passage names the faculty they were not using. Classical commentators observe that the same triad of hearing, sight and hearts appears at several points in the Quran, always in the context of what was given and what was done with it, and that here it follows immediately on a description of people who did not respond to affliction.

keyTerms.note: A word for the heart as the seat of understanding, from a root suggesting heat and movement. The Quran pairs it with hearing and sight as a third instrument of knowledge rather than of feeling.
A verb for spreading seed or offspring widely. It makes human increase an act of sowing, which is why the gathering in the same ayah reads as a harvest rather than as a summons.
The verb for driving people together into one place from all directions, used of herds and of armies. It is the exact reverse of the scattering named in the first half of the sentence.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Hearing was the primary channel of everything that mattered. Poetry, news, genealogy, contracts and the recitation itself all arrived through the ear, in a society where very few read. Naming hearing before sight was not an accident of order. It put first the faculty through which the message was actually reaching them, and which the preceding ayat had just described going unused.
studies.didYouKnow: The same two statements appear together in another surah, in the same order: the making of hearing, sight and hearts in one ayah, and the scattering of people across the earth in the next. Two chapters set the identical pair side by side, once ending in a reproach about thanks and once in a question about when the promise will come.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The faculties are described as produced for you, which makes them a provision rather than equipment a creature simply has. That framing turns their use into a form of thanks and their disuse into ingratitude, which is why the reproach follows immediately and needs no argument. The second sentence then places the whole span of a life, from scattering to gathering, inside the same single agency.

crossReferences.why: Gives the identical pair of statements in the same order, in another Meccan surah.
Says the same faculties were given at birth, when a person knew nothing at all.
Makes hearing, sight and the heart each answerable, which assumes they were given for use.

studies.applyIt: Spend one minute today listening deliberately to whatever is around you, with your eyes shut. Traffic, a kettle, someone in another room. It is an ordinary faculty and it is doing something extraordinarily complicated for free. Thanks is easier to find for things you have just paid attention to than for things you were told to be thankful for.

studies.title: His Is The Turning Of Night
studies.meaning: The third statement in the series is the shortest and reaches furthest. He is the one who gives life and causes death, and to Him belongs the alternation of night and day. Then the question that closes it: will you not use your minds. The commentators note that the alternation is said to belong to God rather than to be made by Him, which puts the daily turning of the sky in the same grammatical relation as a possession.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has been arguing for resurrection against people who found it absurd, and this ayah supplies the analogy without stating it. Classical commentators observe that the alternation of night and day is one of the Quran's standing signs, and note that this is the only place where it is put in the possessive rather than described as something created or made to differ.

keyTerms.note: From the verb for one thing coming after another in place of it, the same root that gives the word for disagreement. What is named is a taking of turns rather than a mere difference.
Placed before the verb for causing death, so the sequence begins with life rather than ending with it. The Quran keeps this order almost everywhere the two verbs appear together.
From a root meaning to tie or tether, as a hobble holds a camel. Reasoning is pictured as restraint that keeps a thing from wandering, not as cleverness or speculation.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Life in Arabia was organised by the turn from night to day and back. Travel happened in the dark, work at the edges of the heat, and the month was read off the moon by anyone who looked up. The alternation was not scenery; it was the clock, the calendar and the schedule at once, and its absolute reliability was the reason all three worked.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for the alternation of night and day occurs five times in the Quran, and four of those put it in a list of things created. This is the only place where it is stated as belonging to God, in the possessive. A phrase the Book normally uses to describe a sign is used here to describe a possession.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Life, death and the turning of the sky are named in one breath and assigned to one owner, and no argument is offered between them. The connection is left for the reader to make, which is what the closing question is for. If the daily replacement of light by dark and back belongs to Him, the replacement of life by death and back is the same operation at a different scale.

crossReferences.why: Names the same alternation as a sign for people of understanding, alongside the heavens and earth.
Brings the living from the dead and the dead from the living, and calls it the way you will be brought out.
Puts the alternation of night and day among the signs for people who guard themselves.

studies.applyIt: Watch one sunset this week from beginning to end without doing anything else. It takes about fifteen minutes and you have almost certainly never done it. The ayah asks you to use your mind on this, and using your mind on something you have not actually looked at is not really available.

studies.title: Legends Of The Ancients
studies.meaning: Instead of answering, they repeat. They said the like of what the earlier people said, and the quotation follows: when we are dead and dust and bones, are we really to be raised. We and our fathers were promised this before; these are nothing but tales of the ancients. Then the surah changes tactic entirely and asks a question of its own. Say: whose is the earth and everyone on it, if you happen to know.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The charge that the recitation was old stories was a standing Meccan objection, recorded in several surahs, and the classical commentators attribute it particularly to men who had heard older scriptural material on the trade routes. The reply that begins here runs for several ayat and is built entirely of questions the audience could not answer any other way.

keyTerms.note: From the root for writing in lines. The word implies something recorded and handed down rather than invented, so the objection is that the material is old and borrowed rather than false.
Used twice in these ayat, first of the peoples who made this same objection and then of the ancients whose stories are being dismissed. The word cuts both ways in the space of three lines.
A question of ownership, not of origin. The reply that follows will accept their answer as given, which is why the question is framed around something they already concede.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca was full of transmitted stories. Traders came back from Syria and Yemen with material about earlier peoples, and there were men in the city who had collected such things and could hold a night gathering with them. Calling the recitation old tales was not a wild accusation in that setting. It was a plausible classification, made by people who knew the genre and could name its dealers.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for earlier peoples appears twice within three ayat and does opposite work each time. First the current generation is said to repeat what the earlier people said, which makes them derivative. Then they dismiss the message as tales of the earlier people, which makes it derivative. The same word carries the surah's charge and their own.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument changes shape at the last ayah, and the change is the point. Having recorded an objection that could be repeated indefinitely, the passage stops answering and starts asking, about something the audience had never disputed. That moves the dispute from what the message is to what they already believe, which is a different kind of argument and one they cannot decline to enter.

crossReferences.why: Records the same accusation, that the recitation is old tales written down and dictated.
Gives the objection in the mouth of people who claim they could produce the like of it themselves.
Repeats the objection about dust and bones almost word for word, with the same closing dismissal.

studies.applyIt: Notice when you win an argument by naming what something is rather than dealing with what it says. That is just politics, that is what they always say, that is old news. It is an efficient move and it does no thinking at all. Once today, refuse yourself the label and answer the actual claim.

studies.title: They Will Say To God
studies.meaning: The answer to the first question is supplied in advance: they will say, to God. Then a follow-up, will you not remember, and immediately another question. Who is Lord of the seven heavens and the mighty throne. The same answer, another follow-up, and then a third question about in whose hand the dominion of everything lies, who grants protection and against whom none is granted. The commentators note that the sequence introduces no new information at all.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, addressed to people who already acknowledged one supreme God and turned to intermediaries alongside Him. Classical commentators note that the Quran repeatedly builds arguments on this admission rather than against it, and that the anticipated answers here are given in the future tense: they will say, which assumes the response and reasons forward from it.

keyTerms.note: An intensified form of the ordinary word for kingship, used only a handful of times in the Quran. The added weight in the word makes it cover the inner workings of things as well as their rule.
The exact word for the Arabian institution by which a person under threat was taken into a clan's protection. The ayah says He grants it and that none can be granted it against Him.
The seat of rule. The commentators affirm it as real without describing how, and read the descriptions attached to it in the Quran as expressing sovereignty rather than a shape or a place.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Protection was a formal institution. A man in danger could seek the protection of a chief, and once it was granted, harming him meant war with that whole clan. It was announced publicly and honoured even between enemies. The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) himself re-entered Mecca once under such an arrangement. The word in this ayah is that exact procedure, applied at a scale where nobody can offer it against God.
studies.didYouKnow: The anticipated answer, they will say to God, appears three times in this surah and nowhere else in the Quran. Two of the three fall in these ayat and the third follows immediately after. Each is closed by a different question, so the same concession is made to yield three separate consequences in the space of five lines.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Nothing is being taught in this passage; something is being extracted. Every premise is one the audience already holds, and the conclusion follows from their own admission rather than from any new claim. That is a particular way of arguing about God, and it locates the problem in inconsistency rather than in ignorance, which is exactly what the third question names when it asks how they are enchanted.

crossReferences.why: Runs the same method, asking questions whose answers the audience concedes and then drawing the conclusion.
Asks who provides and who governs, receives the same answer, and asks why they still turn away.
Grants that they name God as creator and then asks about what they call on besides Him.

studies.applyIt: Write down one thing you say you believe and one thing you did this week that does not fit it. Do not resolve the gap today. Most of us are not short of information; we are carrying an inconsistency we have never put on the same page. Putting it there is the entire exercise.

studies.title: Then How Are You Enchanted
studies.meaning: The third answer comes back the same as the first two, and the closing question is the sharpest of the three. Then how are you bewitched. The commentators read it as asking what has been done to their judgement, since nothing is wrong with their premises and nothing is wrong with the conclusion. Then the verdict, stated flatly: We have brought them the truth, and they are liars. The charge is not error but knowing denial.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The accusation of sorcery had been made repeatedly against the recitation and against the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) by the city's leadership, and the classical commentators note that this ayah returns the word to them. The people who explained the message as enchantment are asked what has enchanted them, using the same vocabulary they had been circulating.

keyTerms.note: A passive verb from the root for magic, and this form occurs only here. Being under a spell means holding true premises and reaching no conclusion from them, which is what the question describes.
The word covers both what is true and what is due, so bringing the truth is also delivering something owed. The passage uses it as the thing supplied rather than as a claim being argued for.
The emphatic form, with two markers of certainty attached. It names a fault of the will rather than of the mind, which is why it follows a sequence in which nobody made a mistake.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Sorcery was a working explanation in that world. Illness, sudden reversals, a man behaving out of character, and a marriage that failed were all things a spell could account for. Accusing someone of magic was therefore not abuse but a diagnosis with social consequences, and it was the standard explanation offered in Mecca for why people who heard the recitation kept changing their lives.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb in this closing question occurs nowhere else in the Quran in this form. It comes from the same root as the accusation of sorcery that the city was making about the message. The passage takes the word its opponents had chosen and turns it into a question about their own reasoning, in the last line of a three-part argument built entirely on their own answers.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage draws a distinction the rest of the surah has been circling. Correct beliefs are held, correct answers are given, and nothing follows from either. That is presented as the actual condition of unbelief in a place like Mecca: not a rival theology but a disconnection between what people would affirm and what they do. Calling it enchantment names the strangeness of that without explaining it away.

crossReferences.why: Records the same concession, that they name God as their creator, and asks how they are turned away.
Shows the accusation of magic being made even about a book they could touch with their hands.
Describes people rejecting signs their own souls were convinced of, out of injustice and arrogance.

studies.applyIt: Pick something you know to be true and have not acted on. Not a big thing. The appointment, the message you owe someone, the habit you have already decided about. Do the smallest possible part of it today. Knowing without acting is common enough that this ayah gives it a name, and the cure is always the same size.

studies.title: Each God Would Take His Own
studies.meaning: Two denials and then a reason. God has not taken a son, and there is no other god with Him. Otherwise each god would have gone off with what he created, and some would have overcome others. The commentators note that the argument runs through creation rather than through power: ownership follows making, so multiple makers would mean multiple estates and, sooner or later, a contest between them. The ayah ends by putting God beyond the descriptions altogether.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The city's religion did not deny a supreme God but placed other figures alongside Him, and it also spoke of divine daughters. Classical commentators note that this ayah addresses both at once, and that its argument is not that the other figures are weak but that a universe holding together as this one does could not be the joint estate of several independent makers.

keyTerms.note: The plain verb for departing, with what he made. The image is domestic rather than cosmic: a partnership dissolving, each party taking his own property away with him when it ends.
From the root for rising above, the same root used earlier in this surah of Pharaoh's court. Division into estates is followed by one party climbing over another, which the ayah treats as inevitable.
The verb for setting out a description of something. The closing phrase places God beyond what is described rather than beyond what is imagined, which keeps the criticism aimed at their speech.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca was governed by partnership and it knew how partnerships end. Caravans were financed by several backers, sanctuary functions were divided among clans, and every arrangement worked until a dispute over shares. Everyone had watched a joint venture split, with each partner withdrawing his own stock. The ayah's argument is made in the commercial logic the audience used daily, applied to the heavens.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase that closes this ayah, placing God beyond what people describe, appears twice in the Quran in exactly this form. Its other occurrence closes a long passage in another Meccan surah that also deals with claims about divine offspring. Both times it arrives after an argument rather than before one, as the conclusion rather than the premise.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The unity of God is argued from the unity of the world, which is a claim available to anyone who looks at it. That is different from asserting it and different from proving it by scripture. The passage also declines to insult the alternatives; it grants them creative power hypothetically and shows what would follow. What is ruled out is not their strength but the coherence of the arrangement.

crossReferences.why: Makes the same argument in one clause: gods other than God in the heavens and earth would have ruined them.
Says that other gods would have sought a way to the owner of the throne, the contest named here.
Closes with the same phrase placing God beyond what people attribute to Him.

studies.applyIt: Look for the single thing today: the way one system runs your day, one body carries you, one set of rules holds a room together. Coherence is so ordinary that it is invisible, and this ayah is built entirely on it. Notice one place where things fit and would not if two parties were in charge of them.

studies.title: Do Not Place Me Among Them
studies.meaning: God is named as knower of what is hidden and what is witnessed, exalted above what they associate. Then a prayer is put in the Prophet's mouth, and its shape is unusual. My Lord, if You show me what they are promised, then my Lord, do not place me among the wrongdoing people. The commentators note what is not asked. He does not ask to be spared the sight, and he does not ask for their punishment; he asks about where he will be standing.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The classical commentators read the repetition of the address in the second ayah as the sentence restarting itself, a feature of the prayer rather than an accident of style. They note that the request is made while the outcome is still distant, and that the answer given immediately after concerns God's ability rather than His intention, leaving the timing entirely open.

keyTerms.note: A pair covering everything, what is hidden from creatures and what is open to them. Naming both together denies that God's knowledge has the shape of ours, which has one of the two and not the other.
An emphatic conditional, so the prayer treats the sight as a real possibility rather than a remote one. What follows the condition is not a plea for escape but a request about company.
Said twice, once in each ayah, so the address restarts before the request. The commentators read the repetition as urgency, the way a person repeats a name before saying the hard part.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Collective punishment was how that world worked. When a clan was raided, everyone in the camp took the consequences, guilty or not, and being present at the wrong tent on the wrong night was enough. Nobody had to explain why standing among a group was dangerous. The prayer asks for something an Arabian listener would have recognised as the most practical possible request.
studies.didYouKnow: The prayer given here asks about placement rather than about rescue, and the answer that follows does not grant it or refuse it. It says instead that God is able to show him what they are promised. A request about where he will stand is met with a statement about what can be shown, and the surah moves on without resolving either.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things are established side by side. God knows the hidden and the visible without difference, and even the messenger asks not to be placed among the wrongdoers. The second is the more striking. It denies that anyone holds a guaranteed position by role or by service, and it makes the request a matter of ongoing asking rather than of settled status.

crossReferences.why: Records people asking not to be placed among the wrongdoing people, in almost the same words.
Names God as knower of the unseen and the witnessed, in the same pairing used here.
Tells the Prophet that whether or not he is shown what they are promised, the return is to God.

studies.applyIt: Ask once this week not to end up in the company you are drifting towards. Not about a person, about a direction. Most of what we become is decided by who we are standing near when it matters, and this prayer treats that as the thing worth asking about rather than the outcome itself.

studies.title: Repel With What Is Better
studies.meaning: An instruction and two prayers, and then a scene. Push back the bad with what is better, and leave the accounting of what they say where it belongs. Then two requests for refuge: from the promptings of the devils, and from their presence. The commentators note the second, which asks not only for protection from what they suggest but from their being near. Then the passage shifts, without warning, to a man at his death asking to be sent back.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The passage closes a long section in which the surah has answered accusations, and the instruction to repel with better arrives at the point where the provocation is at its highest. The classical sources report no specific occasion. The community was being insulted publicly and daily, and the ayat give them something to do with the impulse to answer in kind.

keyTerms.note: A verb of physical pushing, not of enduring. What is asked is an action taken against the harm rather than the absorption of it, and the instrument named is something better.
A plural for a poke or a spur, the small pressure that starts something moving. It names the mechanism as a nudge rather than a command, which is why the second prayer asks about proximity.

The verb is in the plural though he is addressing his Lord, and the commentators explain it variously as a form of urgency or as an address to those present. The plural is one of the most discussed details in the surah.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Answering an insult was not optional in that culture; it was owed. A man who let a slight pass was understood to have accepted it, and his clan felt the loss with him. Poets were kept partly to answer other poets. Telling believers to push back with something better did not tell them to do nothing, which is why the instruction could be heard at all in that setting.
studies.didYouKnow: The two prayers are given in the second person as words to be said, and they have been used as a formula ever since. Their order is unusual: the first asks about the suggestion and the second about the presence, which is the reverse of the sequence in which the trouble arrives. The passage then cuts to a deathbed with no transition at all.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The instruction and the prayers work on two different fronts, and the passage treats them as one problem. What comes from outside is answered by acting better; what comes from inside is answered by asking for protection, because it cannot be argued with. That division is practical rather than doctrinal. The deathbed scene that follows then supplies the reason for urgency, since the one thing the man asks for is the time the reader still has.

crossReferences.why: The same instruction with its result named, and the same prayer for refuge attached.
Names the same prompting and describes the mindful remembering and then seeing.
Another request for delay at death, refused because the term is fixed.

studies.applyIt: The next time somebody is rude to you in a small way, do not swallow it and do not return it. Do a third thing: give them something specific and better within the same hour, and say nothing about why. The ayah uses a verb of pushing, not of enduring, so the instruction is to act rather than to absorb.

studies.title: A Barrier Until They Are Raised
studies.meaning: The request from the deathbed finishes: so that I may act rightly in what I left behind. The answer is a single syllable of refusal, and then an explanation that is almost gentle. It is only a word he is saying. The commentators read that as meaning the request is speech without substance, made by someone who would not in fact act differently. Then the passage closes the door with an image: behind them is a barrier until the day they are raised.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has been arguing with people who denied resurrection outright, and this scene answers them by showing the moment the denial ends. Classical commentators note that the request is for return rather than for mercy, and that the Quran records it several times in almost the same words, always refused, and always made by someone who had already been given time.

keyTerms.note: Something set between two things to keep them apart. The word occurs three times in the Quran, and the other two describe a barrier between two bodies of water that do not mix.
Naming the request as merely a word is the refusal's whole reasoning. What is denied is not its sincerity in the moment but that anything would follow from granting it.
The verb for leaving something undone as much as for leaving a place. The regret is specifically about what was not done, which is the form regret takes when time is what has run out.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Deathbeds in that society were crowded and public. A dying man settled debts, named an heir, released a claim or admitted one, and the words spoken then carried real weight in front of witnesses. Everyone had stood in such a room. The passage borrows that setting exactly, and then shows a request made in it that the usual authority to make such requests does not cover.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the barrier in this ayah occurs three times in the Quran. Its other two uses describe the boundary between two seas, fresh and salt, that meet without mixing. The same term names a division in water and a division in time, and in both cases it describes two things touching along a line neither one crosses.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The refusal is explained rather than simply issued, which matters. It does not say the request comes too late in a merely procedural sense; it says the request is empty, because the willingness expressed at the end was available all along and was not used. The barrier that follows removes the possibility of any further attempt, and the passage names the whole interval rather than only the moment of death.

crossReferences.why: Records the same request to be returned and states that they would go back to what they were forbidden.
Describes the same plea for a delay and says that God never delays a soul once its term has come.
Uses the same word for the barrier, there between two seas that meet and do not overrun each other.

studies.applyIt: Name one thing you would want more time for if you were told today was the last of it. Then do a small piece of it before the week ends. Not the whole thing, and not as a response to fear. The passage's argument is that the willingness at the end was already available, and the only way to test that is to spend some of it now.

studies.title: No Kinship Between Them
studies.meaning: The trumpet is blown and the first thing named is a loss: no lineages between them that day, and they do not ask after one another. Then the scales, in two matching sentences. Whose weights are heavy are the successful; whose are light have lost themselves and remain in the fire. The commentators note the phrase for that loss, which is not that they lost something but that they lost themselves. The last ayah describes the faces, scorched and drawn back.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, addressed to a society in which lineage decided almost everything. Classical commentators read the removal of kinship as answering a specific Meccan confidence, the assumption that clan standing would carry a man through anything. They note that the ayah does not say relations cease to exist, only that they are not between them on that day, and that nobody asks after anybody.

keyTerms.note: The plural of the word for descent, and it occurs only here in the Quran. In a society organised entirely by genealogy, naming its absence was the most economical way to describe a levelling.
The plural can mean the balances or the weights placed in them. The commentators allow both, and either way what is measured is deeds rather than the person doing the weighing.
A face pulled back from the teeth by heat or pain, and the word occurs once in the Quran. It describes an involuntary expression, which is why it says more than any account of feeling would.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Genealogy was the operating system. A man's name carried his father, his clan and his tribe, and reciting a lineage established credit, protection, marriage prospects and the price of his blood. Professional memorisers held the trees. To say there would be no lineages between people was to describe the loss of everything that told a Meccan who he was and who owed him anything.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for kinship ties in this ayah occurs nowhere else in the Quran, and neither does the word for the drawn-back faces three ayat later. The passage brackets its account of the scales with two terms the Book never repeats, one naming what is taken away at the start and one describing what is left at the end.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The loss is described as being of oneself rather than of a reward, which is a specific claim. What the light scales indicate is not a failed transaction but a person who spent a life and has nothing that turned out to be theirs. Removing kinship first makes the point sharper: every borrowed identity is gone, and what is weighed is only what the individual actually did.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same pair of outcomes in the same order, heavy scales and light ones, in a short surah.
Describes each person fleeing from brother, parents and family on that day, the same severing.
Warns that no parent will avail his child and no child his parent on that day.

studies.applyIt: Think of one thing you rely on that you did not earn: a family name, a passport, an accent that opens doors, a network you were born into. You are not asked to give any of it up. Just notice, once, how much of what you think of as yourself is on loan, and what would be left if the loan were called in.

studies.title: Our Wretchedness Overcame Us
studies.meaning: A question is put to them, and it is about a specific thing: were My signs not recited to you, and you kept denying them. Their answer accepts the charge and then reassigns it. Our wretchedness overcame us and we were a people gone astray. Then they ask to be taken out, promising that a return to it would make them wrongdoers. The commentators note the conditional. Even the promise is phrased as a hypothetical rather than as a commitment.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The exchange closes a long sequence in which the same recitation was described as being read to people who turned away, and classical commentators read the question as picking that thread up. They note that no new evidence is presented in the scene, only a reminder of what was already given, and that the answer offered by those addressed contains no denial of the facts.

keyTerms.note: A state of misery and hard luck, and the word occurs once in the Quran. Naming it as the thing that overcame them turns their own condition into an external force with a will of its own.
The verb for winning a contest. Choosing it makes them the losing party in a struggle rather than the ones who decided, which is what the reply that follows declines to accept.
A word used to drive off a dog, and it appears once in the Quran. The commentators do not soften it; it is a dismissal that closes a conversation rather than an answer within one.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Fortune was a real category in Arabian thought, and much of the poetry is about it: time as a force that grinds people down, luck that turns without reason, fate as something a man endures rather than shapes. Blaming misfortune for how a life turned out was not an excuse invented on the spot. It was the standard explanation, and everyone in the audience had used it.
studies.didYouKnow: Two words in this short exchange occur nowhere else in the Quran: the word they use for their own wretchedness and the word of dismissal they receive. One is the excuse and the other is the answer, and the Book uses each exactly once. The dismissal is ordinarily addressed to an animal being driven off rather than to a person.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The request is not refused because repentance is impossible but because there is nothing left to repent from. The scene shows a turning that arrives after the only thing that made turning meaningful, which was the possibility of not turning. Their explanation is also quietly rejected: wretchedness as an overwhelming force is exactly the account the question at the start had already answered, by naming what was recited and what was done with it.

crossReferences.why: Records the same request for a second chance and answers that a warner had already come.
Describes repentance offered at the point of death and says it is not accepted then.
Gives the regret in a soul's own words, wishing for another chance to be among those who do good.

studies.applyIt: Catch yourself blaming a force today. Bad luck, no time, the way you are, how things went. Some of that is true. Then find the smallest part of it that was actually a decision, and name that part out loud. Repentance is not available for what happened to you, and it is available for the part that did not.

studies.title: A Group Of My Servants
studies.meaning: After the dismissal comes an explanation, and it turns entirely on something small. There was a group of My servants who used to say: our Lord, we have believed, so forgive us and have mercy on us, and You are the best of the merciful. The commentators note the tense. It describes a habit rather than an occasion, words said often enough to be what those people were known for, and the surah is about to say what was done to them for it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The earliest followers in the city included many with no clan protection, and reports describe them being ridiculed in public by men of standing. Classical commentators connect this ayah to that situation directly, and note that the group is described by what they said rather than by their names or their tribes, which is the reverse of how Mecca identified anybody.

keyTerms.note: A portion split off from a larger body. The word implies a minority within something rather than a community of its own, which is exactly the position of the people being described.
A form for repeated or continuous action in past time. What is recorded is not a single prayer but a practice, said often enough that it became the identifying mark of the group.
A phrase used twice in the Quran, both times in this surah. It appears here in the mouth of the mocked, and again in the final ayah of the chapter as words the Prophet is told to say.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca decided who mattered by descent and wealth, and the early community drew heavily from people who had neither: freed slaves, clients attached to stronger families, young men without inheritance. Such people were not physically safe and were routinely humiliated in the open. Being identified by a sentence you repeated, rather than by a father's name, was not a distinction that city knew how to award.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase these servants use, calling God the best of the merciful, occurs twice in the Quran and both times in this surah. Its second appearance is the surah's final ayah, where the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) is instructed to say almost exactly the same words. The chapter ends by giving him the prayer of the people who were laughed at.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reason given for their standing is a sentence, not an achievement. They believed, they asked for forgiveness, and they acknowledged mercy as belonging to God in the highest degree. Nothing about power, numbers or vindication appears in it. Placing that speech at the centre of the scene makes the surah's whole argument turn on what a group of unimportant people were in the habit of saying.

crossReferences.why: Closes this surah with almost the same prayer, given to the Prophet as words to say.
Records believers saying that they have believed, so forgive us, in a closely matching form.
Moses uses a closely related phrase, calling God the most merciful of those who show mercy.

studies.applyIt: Pick a short prayer and say it enough times this month that it becomes yours. Not a long one; the one in this ayah is a single line. What the passage records about these people is not a great act but a habit of speech, kept up while they were being laughed at, and habits are built by repetition rather than by intensity.

studies.title: You Took Them For A Joke
studies.meaning: The charge is laid out in sequence. You took them as a laughing matter, until that made you forget My remembrance, and you used to laugh at them. The commentators note the middle clause, which is the mechanism: mockery is not only cruel but occupying, and the attention it takes is attention taken from something else. Then the verdict, in the first person and dated to that day. I have rewarded them today for their patience; they are the ones who have won.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Reports describe the leading men of the city treating the early followers as entertainment, pointing them out to visitors and mimicking them in gatherings. Classical commentators connect this passage to that practice, and note that the reward named here is for endurance specifically, not for any action the mocked group took in reply.

keyTerms.note: Something taken as a butt of jokes. The word appears twice in the Quran, and its other use is in a scene where people search the fire for those they had ridiculed and cannot find them.
The grammar makes the mocked group the cause of the forgetting, which the commentators read as an effect rather than an act. Being absorbed in ridiculing someone is what displaced the remembrance.
From the root for attaining a prize or escaping danger. The word is announced with emphasis, and it names the outcome of a contest that the other party did not know they were in.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mockery was a weapon with a technique. Satirical poetry could destroy a man's standing across the peninsula in a season, and skilled lampooners were feared more than fighters. A group who could be laughed at publicly and could not answer in kind had no protection at all in that system. What the passage describes is not idle unkindness but the standard method of dealing with a threat.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for taking someone as a laughing matter appears twice in the Quran. Its other use is in a scene set in the fire, where people ask what became of the men they used to count among the worst and had taken as a joke, and wonder whether their eyes have simply missed them. Both passages put the mockery in the past tense.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reward is given for patience and nothing else, which sets the terms of a very common situation. The mocked group is not described as having answered back, prevailed, or been vindicated in their lifetimes. What is recorded is that they endured, and the verdict on that is announced by God directly rather than reported. The mockers, meanwhile, lost something without noticing they were spending it.

crossReferences.why: Puts the same word in the mouths of people searching for those they used to ridicule.
Describes the same pattern at length, and reverses who is laughing at whom in the end.
States that messengers before were mocked, and that what they ridiculed closed in on them.

studies.applyIt: Notice how much of your attention this week goes to disliking someone. The scrolling, the retelling, the small pleasure of a joke at their expense. This ayah says that occupation is itself the cost, before any question of whether the mockery was deserved. Reclaim ten minutes of it and put them somewhere else.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: A Day, Or Part Of A Day
studies.meaning: A question is put and the answer collapses a lifetime. Asked how many years they stayed on earth, they say a day or part of a day and then defer to those who keep count, which the commentators read as a sign that even the estimate has gone. The reply corrects them downward: only a little. Then comes the question the whole passage was built for, whether they thought they were created for nothing and would not be returned.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, at the very end of the surah, after a scene in which those who had mocked the believers are told what their mockery earned. The exchange about years belongs to the Day rather than to any moment in Mecca. No specific occasion is reported. The final question is addressed past the scene to the listener, which is how the surah closes its argument.

keyTerms.note: A participle for people whose work is counting, used of accountants and of those who reckon days. Deferring to them is an admission that the speaker's own sense of duration has failed entirely.
A word for aimless play or fiddling, action with no purpose behind it. The question is not whether life is difficult but whether it is idle, which is a different and sharper accusation to answer.

A verb of remaining somewhere for a time. In a culture that measured a man's life in the raids and seasons he had seen, reducing all of it to a day is the strongest available way of saying it went fast.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Nobody knew their exact age. Births were placed by reference to events, the year of the elephant or the year of a famous drought, and a man's years were an approximation everybody accepted. Only specialists kept running counts, for debts and for the sacred months. So deferring to those who keep count was an ordinary thing to say, and the ayah puts it in the mouths of people at the end of everything.
studies.didYouKnow: The surah opens by declaring believers successful and closes by asking whether creation was pointless, so the first and last movements answer each other. The word for aimless play used here occurs only once in the Quran. And the very last ayah of the chapter is a prayer for forgiveness and mercy, which follows the question without any argument between them.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument moves from duration to purpose in one step, and the step is the point. If a lifetime can be reported as a day, then its significance cannot lie in its length, which leaves only what it was for. The question is then put as a question rather than a statement, so the reader has to supply the answer. And the alternative offered is stark: either created in vain, or returned. Nothing in between is proposed.

crossReferences.why: The same exchange with a different estimate: ten days, or one.
Puts the same question directly: does a person think he is left without purpose.
Gives the answer the question implies, naming worship as the purpose of creation.

studies.applyIt: Work out how many days you have been alive. It takes ten seconds on a phone and the number is larger than you expect and smaller than it should be. Then leave it. The ayah does not ask you to do anything with the figure. It asks whether you have ever thought about what the whole thing was for.

studies.title: Forgive And Have Mercy
studies.meaning: The surah gathers itself. God is exalted, the true King, no god but He, Lord of the noble throne. Then a statement about anyone who calls on another god without proof: his reckoning is with his Lord, and those who refuse do not succeed. And then the last line of the chapter, which is not an argument at all. Say: my Lord, forgive and have mercy, and You are the best of the merciful. The commentators note that the surah ends by asking rather than by concluding.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the closing movement of a chapter that has run through four rejected messengers, a long argument about resurrection, and a scene of judgement. Classical commentators observe that the final ayah gives the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) the same words the mocked believers were quoted saying a few ayat earlier, and read the repetition as deliberate closure rather than as coincidence.

keyTerms.note: A pairing used twice in the Quran. The second word means both real and rightful, so the title claims that this kingship is the actual one and that others hold the name without the substance.
A word for evidence that settles a matter, stronger than an argument. Its absence is what the ayah names, so the objection to calling on another god is put as a failure of evidence.
From a root meaning to split open ground for planting, so success is pictured as a farmer's return rather than as a windfall. The same verb opens this surah in its first ayah.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Kings were known to Mecca by report and by trade: the Persian court, the Byzantine emperor, the ruler in Abyssinia who had given shelter to some of the early believers. Every one of them was a real power and every one of them could be outlived. Calling God the true King in that setting was making a comparison the audience could run through in their heads with actual names.
studies.didYouKnow: The surah opens with the verb for success in its first ayah, declaring the believers successful, and closes with the same verb negated, saying that those who refuse do not succeed. The chapter is bracketed by one root used twice in opposite directions. Its very last words are the prayer that the mocked believers had been quoted saying a few ayat earlier.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Everything the chapter established is placed behind a request rather than in front of a conclusion. Having named God as the true King and stated that refusal does not prosper, the surah's final act is to ask for forgiveness and mercy, and to name God as the best at giving them. That order says something about where confidence properly ends. The argument is finished and the asking is not.

crossReferences.why: Opens this surah with the same verb for success, declared of the believers in the completed tense.
Uses the same title for God, the true King, alongside a prayer for an increase in knowledge.
Gives the same closing prayer earlier in this surah, in the mouths of servants who were ridiculed.

studies.applyIt: End something today with a request rather than a verdict. A conversation you were about to win, a piece of work you were about to sign off, a day you were about to summarise to yourself. Say the surah's last line instead, in your own words, and let that be the last thing rather than your conclusion about how it all went.
